title: Classical Adversarial Fault-Tolerance and PCPs
abstract: We show how to compile an arbitrary classical circuit into a fault-tolerant circuit, which performs the desired computation even when an almost-linear number of bits are adversarially chosen and corrupted in each timestep. Using a variant of this fault-tolerance scheme that only detects (rather than corrects) corruptions, we give a new construction of probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) for NP with polylogarithmic query complexity. This PCP construction from fault-tolerance presents a promising candidate for quantization by the work of Anshu, Breuckmann, and Nguyen (STOC'24), who provided a roadmap for constructing quantum PCPs via fault-tolerance.

bite.hook: Compile an arbitrary classical circuit into a fault-tolerant circuit robust against an almost-linear number of corrupted bits.
tldr: We compiled an arbitrary classical circuit into a fault-tolerant circuit that handles an almost-linear number of adversarially corrupted bits per timestep.
We used a variant of this fault-tolerance scheme that only detects corruptions rather than correcting them.
We constructed new probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) for NP with polylogarithmic query complexity.
bite.whyItMatters: This breakthrough bridges classical fault tolerance and proof verification, offering a promising foundation for building quantum PCPs.
bite.eli5: Imagine trying to send a secret message through a room full of pranksters who swap out letters. This paper shows how to wrap your message in special error-detecting armor so you can still read the original intent even if a huge fraction of it gets messed with maliciously.

glossary.shortDef: A network of logic gates that process bits to perform a computation.
glossary.eli5Def: A maze of tiny switches that takes input data and flips them around to calculate an answer.

glossary.shortDef: Proofs that can be verified by checking only a few randomly chosen parts.
glossary.eli5Def: A massive homework book that a teacher can grade correctly by just spot-checking three random lines.

glossary.shortDef: Growing at a rate bounded by a polynomial in the logarithm of the input size.
glossary.eli5Def: A growth rate that stays extremely small even when the problem gets immensely huge.
